TELL ME ABOUT YOUR FAMILY AND ALL. TELL ME ABOUT GROWING UP IN LITTLE ROCK. WHAT GOT YOU STARTED ON MUSIC?

My Grand-dad was the head of a committee that bought up a gang of instruments and gave them to the high schools. By my grand-dad being the head of the committee I had my choice of any instrument I wanted in the band. So, I choose the trombone as a little kid. In fact, I have a little picture of me when I first started. I was only playing about two or three months. That's how I started---in the high school band.
WHAT HIGH SCHOOL WAS THIS?
Gibbs High School in Little Rock, Arkansas.
WAS ANYBODY ELSE IN HIGH SCHOOL WITH YOU. OR ANYBODY ELSE LIKE THAT IN HIGH SCHOOL WITH YOU?
No but I knew , he had played with
HE'S OLDER THAN YOU.

Yes, he's older than I am. But another guy, Happy Johnson, a trombone player. We both picked bones the same day. He only lived about two blocks from my house in Little Rock. He got to be a pretty good name.
HE DID PRETTY WELL OUT IN CALIFORNIA.
Yes. He did very well.

SO IN OTHER WORDS, WHEN YOU WERE IN HIGH SCHOOL NOW, YOU HAD TO DEVELOP YOUR OWN STYLE BECAUSE I DON'T THINK THERE WAS ANYBODY ELSE AROUND THEN--NO OUTSTANDING TROMBONE PLAYER IN LITTLE ROCK WAS THERE AT THAT TIME.
Well-, there was a guy with the Rose City Orchestra called Saxton. His real name was Will Parish.
HE CAME HERE TO PLAY WITH CHICK WEBBLATER?
Yeah, he did play with Chick awhile.
HE WAS INSIDE ROSE CITY ORCHESTRA?
Yeah-, right-, he had later became a Red Cap down here.
IS HE STILL LIVING?

No, he died. He is about the only trombone player that I liked. Although I did not try to copy after him. In fact, I was determined, when I picked up the trombone, to do my own thing. I was determined not to play like anybody; so, I just practiced day and night. In fact, I practiced so much that they thought I was going to go nuts. So they took me off the instrument for a time.
WHAT OPPORTUNITIES DID YOU HAVE TO PLAY WHEN YOU WRE IN SCHOOL? DID YOU HAVE MUCH OPPORTUNITY TO PLAY OTHER THAN PRACTICE OR WERE YOU PLAYING TYPICAL SCHOOL...

Well, we were playing typical band music. I never forget a time that I put a couple of extra notes in this band music and Mr. Cook, the band master, hit me over my head with a baton. I shall never forget that. But, I always wanted to be what we call swing. I always wanted to do that.
YOU DIDN'T HAVE TO MUCH FEAR OUT OF COMING OUT OF LITTLE ROCK; DID YOU?
The only jazz thing that was going on in Little Rock then was the Grove Street Orchestra under Sterling Todd.
THAT'S A PIANO PLAYER.
A piano player, right.
YEAH!
He later went to Chicago.
WHERE DID THEY PLAY AT?
Well he's played at the different affairs and-
THERE WERE NO NIGHT CLUBS OR ANYTHING IN LITTLE ROCK.
There were no night clubs.
WASN'T ANYTHING LIKE THAT. No-, there was no night clubs when I was coming up.
I HEARD ABOUT THAT. He was a great musician. Great musician.
WHAT TYPE OF BAND WAS IT. LEADING BAND. ALL LEADING BAND? It was a leading band.
DIDN'T PLAY TOO MUCH INTER-RELATIONS? No too much, but they did some. Especially on souls. They had some pretty good souls. Joe Haymen later joined the band. He was with them for a while.
WHO ELSE? Slazie went into there too. We came up together.
HIS WIFE IS STILL HERE. She called me last year. Wasn't it last year?

Yeah-, but I don't think she was with the show.
OH MAYBE... MAYBE NOT; I DON'T KNOW.
No, she just went with him.

Well-, I ran into a guy, Eugene Cook.
MY BUDDY, YEAH!
(Laughing.) Well- Eugene Cook. Ugh-

Trent was with him.
TRENT WAS WORKING WITH HIM.

With him. Cook heard me play. We did a parade out at sweet home and somebody pointed this guy out to me. This guy had a band and I decided that my life wasn't going to be made with this band; so I put my X-notes in there. I played, I played, I played. I put my things in there. When it got down to solo, I played me a swing solo. Which Mr.
Cook didn't like it all. But I didn't care because I wanted to impress Cook, and obviously I did because he hired me to come into the band and we went down to Hellener, Arkansas.
We were playing at a drug store.
A drug store.
Well-, what happened, he gave us a certain amount of money. In other words he guaranteed our food and lodging, and then we got most of our extra money as a service through the hat.
Sometimes we played out on the sidewalk right in front of the drug store.
This was day time, yes.

That went on for at least a couple of months.
YEAH.
Yeah.

It was summertime.

I think he had six. He had six in the band.

To drag me back.

A summer resort, yeah and A.G. impressed everybody, you know he was fantastic

Yes.

One of the greatest who ever picked up a stick.

He fired his cousin and put A.G. in there. And nobody blamed him. I don't think his cousin blamed. His cousin was spellbound by A.G.-------

Well yes. Cook...

No. Cook was much older, but he didn't have very much business . Then Tripp was very wealthy too you know.

Well, he , at one time they had 100 rent houses. His family had rows of houses called Trent's Row.

Fort Smith, right. Well after we played Stem Beach that summer I had to still go back to school. Yeah and Trent brought the band to Little Rock and stayed around Little Rock so that I could be with the band. I appreciated it very much.
HE COULD AFFORD TO STAY AROUND THERE EVEN THOUGH THERE WASN'T THAT MUCH WORK?
That's right.
HIS FAMILY HAD THE MONEY. THEY INDULGED HIM TO KEEP HIS THING TOGETHER.
They gave him anything he wanted.
NOW YOU WEREN'T PLAYING ANY ARRANGEMENTS AT THIS TIME WITH NO ARRANGER IN THIS BAND.
No the only arrangements we had were some arrangements stocks. We had some stocks.
EVERYBODY READ MUSIC IN THE BAND.

Everybody had to read music to join that band. Started to read from the beginning. And that's one thing he insisted upon and later when it got to be a co-op band, we all insisted anybody joining that band had to be a heck of a reader and an improvisor. He had to improvise.
THEN YOU GRADUATED FROM SCHOOL AND FINALLY GET OUT OF HIGH SCHOOL. THEN YOU WERE WITH HIM FULL TIME. THAT'S WHEN YOU GO DOWN TO TEXAS?

ARKANSAS?

And we were

No, I don't remember meeting him. I don't think I knew him until later. You see that band was so outstanding that a lot of the guys who knew me, had been guys who played in the band. Andy Kirk said he met me years ago in Dalls when we did a concert. Well, I didn't remember that.

No, he wasn't. You see because Andy Kirk got his band.

And I getting a little ahead of my story. We played we had to pass the hat in Eldorado. That's how we would eat and that's how we got money to get our room. I'll never forget the nights we passed the hat around and we played on this corner for about 2 hours and the Cats were really playing and we got enough money to get sandwiches and to pay for a room. We would double up and that's how we lived. We didn't know anybody in the band, everybody in the

band was from families that could well-afford to give them what they wanted, but we didn't. We were determined to make it on our own. Anyway, we left there and went into Dallas. And we were playing out a place called Oak Cliff.
Oak Cliff, yeah. And we were playing at this ballroom, big, big ballroom and one of the head bellmen at the -----he was crazy about the band and he had Mr. E----who was the manager have his secretary
Great big guy.

Great big German fellow. Anyway she came out, we always called her Miss Mary and she heard the band and persuaded Mr. E--- to give us a tryout. Then we went down and tried out and he gave us a two week contract.
That was a lily-white hotel.
FROM WHAT I HEARD.

It was such a lily-white hotel, when we went in there we were explained to, he explained to us that we had to abide by the rules. We had to take the back elevator up and we had to take it out. Of course, it's a different story. Everybody stays at the Dallas now and all the other hotels. But we had a two-week contract and the guys were sensational. That was something to, we were the first ones to play for a white audience.
YOU HAD TO BE.

We were. And it created such a sensation all around because nothing but the wealthy came to the A----, but the poor class, especially some of the police department, things like that, they didn't like it and Ku Klux Klan of course they didn't like it. Then we got to a place where I figured it would be advantageous to me in more ways than one that I could make just as much money with the trio and also I'd be able to play more myself. I was criticized for not playing enough in some of my records.
You were emphasizing the show business side a little bit too much.

That's one of the reasons why the records--a lot of the records had not appealed to the jazz people, because of that. They were a little bit too arranged in some cases and there aren't enough solos. The Decca's are probably the best for showing what you can play. The Penguins were too much singing.
On that Sonora, they really--the Man With The Funny Horn was very good, but on the Sonora records--you ought to hear them. Do you have time for me to play them?
Oh, sure.
I want you to hear the execution of the things I did in Social Drag and You Went Too Far and Stayed Too Long.
Who was Sonora; who was that?
It was a big company that had a few million dollars that they just signed up too many people.
Who was recording it for you?
Quite a few; Georgie
Gibbs--
No, I mean who was recording you? Who was the guy that signed you at Sonora?
This was the president of the company; I forget her name.
It was a woman?
A woman, yeah. She got in touch with me. In fact, I guess she looked in the phone book; she sent me this letter to please get in touch.
In the meantime, Dresnon didn't mind it because this is during the time that you were recording for him, for Penguin?
Right.
Did he realize that he could not get that much business on his own label?
That's right.
So he said okay.
That's the reason why I said he was more of a father than a manager.
Because he didn't mind;
No, it didn't bother him at all.
Was he supervising the sessions as well or was somebody else actually in the studio?
I supervised it. He was there but--
I know what we missed; Ben Smith. Now let's get him in the picture. Where do we get Ben Smith?
When I got back from overseas--
The first time; right?
'45. I went into the One Hundred Club.
That's in the Village?
No, no, that's 100 and Broadway. When 100th Street was really swanky.
Broadway and 100th Street?
100th Street and Broadway.
Oh yeah?
The One Hundred Club in the Whitehall Hotel. It's a flea place now, but then it was nothing but swanky. That's where we were broadcasting the Associated Broadcasting System network.
This is 1945?
November, '45.
The band is Bob Carroll; right?
Bob Carroll.
Ben Smith.
Ben Smith.
You; Lloyd Phillips?
No. Smiley Trotman.
Smiley Trotman and Jimmy Robinson.
Jimmy Robinson on bass.
A.G. Godley.
A.G. Godley and then I got a little sick of A.G. for a while and got
Tommy Benford.
I've got a picture of that band. Would you want one of them?
Yeah.
I think you got one of those copied already. This is it right here.
You can keep that.
You, Bob Carroll; is this Jimmy Robinson?
No, no, Jimmy wasn't in the band then.
This is Ed Snead?
Ed Snead.
Who is this?
Frank Cahill.
On alto?
Right.
What place is this now?
This is out at the Flame in Duluth that I was telling you about.
Oh, the Flame in Duluth. The piano player is who?
I forget his name.
This is after Ben Smith and all?
Right.
Ben Smith is gone?
Right.
Ben Smith didn't go out of New York with you, in other words? He didn't go on the road?
Oh yeah. He was down in Maryland.
Where'd you work in Maryland?
Salisbury, Maryland. The nightclub there.
For a while?
Yeah, we worked there for about four months, I guess. We couldn't find any place to eat, we got tired of that.
Now who is Frank Cahill?
He played a pretty nice
horn. I had a hit on Sonora called the Hasty Man.
Was he on that?
He's on that.
This around '47.
That's right, because Snead--I'm pretty sure Snead was the last bass player that Jimmy Lunceford had. Jimmy Lunceford died in '47, so it would have to be '48.
I didn't know he played for Jimmy Lunceford.
Yeah, he did. He came up and took George Duvivier's place.
He did?
Yeah.
George Duvivier made that record with me.
Which one?
Blue Memories.
On Penguin?
Yeah.
He wasn't working with you thought; was he?
Yeah, he made a few dates.
He's the number one man in New York as far as I'm concerned. Where is this, and how late is this? Oh, this is back at the Queens Terrace.
Doesn't that have a date on it?
There's nothing on here but the names. Fauntleroy; he's still around, isn't he?
Yeah, he's around.
Fauntleroy, George Spots, this one I can't quite see.
That's Abie Baker.
That's Abie Baker; yeah. This is Kenny?
Right.
This can't be too late then, unless he worked with you more than once; did he work with you more than once?
No.

Then this has got to be '45 or '46. Yeah, this has to be the same time as this other picture. This is back at the Queens Terrace; this is 1945. So in other words, Spots probably took Buji Ward's place. What happened to Buji, is he still around?
I don't know.
What I was trying to think of, we had this one copied already so there's no problem. How much further---after this, this is out at the Flame, Duluth; right?
That wasn't the time when I was on my way to Hollywood.
No, this was later.
This was way later.
This is '48, maybe '49.

I can tell you exactly. That was taken in almost '47, because my brother died just as I was getting ready to go work. It was in December of '46. This was more likely January of '47, but I opened December of '46.
This is in Duluth?
The Flame Show Bar?
Right. It was a big club though.
I know, because they're still wearing the tuxedos, which is full dress. What I'm trying to do now is figure out--go from '46-'47; where do you go from here? How long did this job last?
That job lasted about three or four months.
Then where did you go from there?
We came back to New York and went out to Farmingdale.
What was out there?
It was one of the finest
clubs, they didn't want us to come in. It was a very fine club but they never had a colored band in there before. I don't remember the name of that club even, but it was a fine club.
I can find out. Was this with the same group of guys?
Yeah.
How long did that job last?
That job lasted about four months.
You did some business out there?
A wonderful business.
This would have been around the time you were recording Hasty Man?
He recorded it with me.
Is he from New York?
He's from New York.
Yeah.
Frank Cahill.
You made quite a few sides for Penguin?
Right. Blue Memories, I've Been a Fool, I'm a Fool About Mama, Could This Be Love, Abrazamae (phonetic spelling).
That's not your tune?
No.
That sounds like a great theme song for you though. In Farmingdale, Dresnon is getting these bookings; right?
Right.
Where do you go from Farmingdale? This is still '47.
In '48 we just played around--
But '48 is a recording band.
But I did play--this bass player, a fat guy, white--
Chubby Jackson.
We played a club of his
out on Long Island, '48--
Same group?
Yeah.
And '49.
Then we went up to Boston and went back into the Tick Tock.
Yeah.
And then from there we booked the Boston show--I had my own show there--
went all the way to Florida. I had my own Greyhound bus.
What kind of show was this, a package show?
A package show.
Singers and dancers?
Yeah.
Do you have a picture of that?
I have a picture, I can find it. I saw one not long ago.
That would be good to
I'll find one. Sam Robbins--Sam and his brother.
What were you playing, clubs or theatres?
We were playing in theatres.
Theatres, really?
Al the way down from here to Florida.
I never heard you mention anything about that before.
I didn't mention that too much.
You probably didn't do too good with it then.
We did fairly well.
Who did you have in the show with you? Anybody else who was a name?
This girl, Evelyn White.
Evelyn White, Baby White? The one who tried to pass herself off as
(Inaudible) daughter?
I don't know.
She used to sing with Claude's band.
Out of Boston?
I'm not sure where she-- Pat Evelyn. She used to work with Savvy Louis.
That's who she is.
Evelyn White; yeah.
A wonderful singer.
Yes, a wonderful singer. Evelyn White.
She was one of the--I used to love to play for her.
We played all the way down to Miami Beach, all the way down through Virginia; every place in Virginia, North Carolina, South Carolina. All the way down to Alabama, to Atlanta, Georgia.
The South was changing at this time, I assume or was it still rough?
It was still rough.
Still no accommodations?
No, we had to sleep in the bus half the time.
Did you make any money with her?
I made some nice money. We got all the way down to Miami Beach and they offered me this job, a very fine job, at a place called Delicate Pines.
In Miami Beach?
Yes. It had about twenty people in the show, a fag half the show, two bands, a fag half went on and then we played for the legitimate show and I stayed there for about five months.
It was December of '49 when we left.
You left Boston in December of '49 to start the tour?
Right.
And the tour lasted, how long would you say the tour lasted?
The tour lasted about three months. And then I stayed for about four months in Miami Beach.
So that would bring you up to the summer of '50, July or August of 1950.
I would say July or August of 1950; right.
At the Delicate Pines was this basically the same guys or was it different guys?
No, I had altogether different guys and I organized over. I had Freddy Jefferson on Piano, I still had Bobby Carroll.
You didn't have Willard Brown back?
No. I got this boy that later got a band of his own, a way out trumpet player.
You said you had Bobby Carroll.
I did have Bobby.
You replaced him?
I replaced him.
Bob Carroll was drinking pretty bad by then?
Yeah.
Way out, way out; not Dizzy Gillespie? Someone like him?
Yeah.
It wasn't Miles Davis?
No, Miles played with me for a while though.
Miles played with you?
Yeah.
When did Miles play with you?
I forget what year it was.
How long did Miles play with you?
About three weeks.
I can't imagine him.
He didn't play way out then.
No, I know he didn't. This would probably be not too long after you came out of the service--not the service--'46 probably.
He came down to see me in the sixties, when I was getting ready to go overseas.
I never knew he played with you.
He played with me for about three weeks.
Here in New York probably?
Yeah.
It must have been in somewhere like the One Hundred Club.
It wasn't in the One Hundred Club, because one of the things about the One Hundred Club, I was broadcasting coast to coast four nights a week, Billy Daniels was a
Norma Shepherd.
Norma Shepherd; it was some club.
They had good clubs on the west side like that for years.
That was some club, we did some business.
So you're saying a far out trumpet player, you say he had his own band?
Something pertaining to color.
Who was playing drums, was A.G. still playing drums with you or not?
Yeah, A.G. was still on drums.
Snead was still with you?
No.
So mostly it was different guys, New York guys?
Yeah.
Where did you go from Delicate--where did you go from there?
We came back east and then we started doing jazz concerts. I broke up the band and we were just playing gigs. I was doing things down like the Stuyvesant Casino.
I remember those days.
I did that and then I got the band back together and went overseas in '52.
So in other words, the rest of '50 and '51, you really were mostly doing single?
Yeah.
'52 is when you organized the band again and played the USO?
Right.
How long did that last?
One year.
That's what I was going to say; it lasted one year.

It lasted one year. I first went to Alaska and stayed thirteen weeks. Sounds funny being a place like that, but we were playing every little place. I had my own plane assigned to me, with a crew. Then we came back here and had a week off and went to Europe.
Yeah, you were in Europe in '53.
And '53.
'52, you're right. The summer of '52.
I got into London June 30. I stayed all of July in England, all over England and went to France in August.
I got a picture of Alberta singing with you in France.
One of the dog gonest things that happened--
How did you come to pick Alberta? Was she already assigned?
She was with the USO.
She's done a lot of USO.

They asked me if it was all right and I said of course. She was much older than the girls that I had, but that was all right with me. I had no trouble with her and we had a rough tour. She did her work.
She's a good show person.

She's as cheap as a nickel whistle, she's got every nickel she ever made and a little story that goes along with all the hard knocks we had, most of the guys got their money, they would get twenty five or thirty dollars and the rest of the money was here for them when they got back and she insisted on getting all of her money; she just liked to pat it. I kept telling her you shouldn't walk around with a thousand dollars and all that, but she just loved it.
We got into Paris and I persuaded

her to go down and get some traveler's checks. So we got in the cab and got out of the cab at American Express, we made about four steps and she screamed, oh, my purse, my purse is in the cab and I ran and screamed and screamed, and I know this guy thought I wish I never stopped for that guy, he heard me and stopped.
You had to make arrangements on her numbers, I assume.
She had her own arrangements.
Oh she had her own arrangements?
Yeah.
For a small band?
We had eight pieces.
When did this USO thing break up? You spent all of August in France.
We spent all of August in France, in Germany September--part of September anyway and then we came back and played New York for a couple of weeks and I did a few gigs that
With this band?
Yeah; I kept everybody together.
You were keeping them together?
Oh, yeah.
These were not steady, these were not long terms jobs, were they?
I had contracts for the whole year.
But that's USO.
USO.
I'm not talking about-- there were no night clubs?
No, I didn't like it. I liked to tour.
We stayed in New York a few weeks and then we went to Korea.
Korea is in '53 mostly, late '52?
That was the end of that thing, wasn't it?
We went to Japan after.
Bud Johnson's on this, isn't he?
Bud Johnson was on the European tour. I took Bernie Peacock.
That's where you got Bernie Peacock and Pruitt; two headaches. It's a wonder they didn't get shot by the enemy over there.

That's when they made me an honorary member of the Second Division. We played at a couple of the EVAC hospitals, right behind the lines, where they would pick them up in the helicopter and bring them back there.
How was Budd on the tour? Budd was all right, wasn't he?
Fine.
He could arrange like
mad too.
He made some arrangements for me too. He made some beautiful arrangements.
When you came back from Korea, that was it, isn't it, for the USO, for the time being?
Yeah, that was it for a while.
When you came out of the USO, that was the last USO trip you made for quite a while, in '53, wasn't it?
Right.
You weren't able to keep the band together after that? In other words, there were no jobs in the nightclubs then for you to keep that eight piece group together.
Not that eight piece group; no.
So what did you do? Is that when you broke back down to a trio?
That's when I went down
to a trio.
Now this was getting close to the time that I met you.
Yeah, you met me in '55, didn't you?
'55. So when you were working the Frolic--
I was working the Frolic in '55.
The Frolic you were in and what was the other--the Sands doesn't come until later, does it?
Part of the time I was working upstate in the Catskills.
I thought you didn't work the Catskills until more recent years.
I worked there the first time in '57--'56 and '57.
Yeah, that's what I thought.
That's the time some guy came over and was talking about Trent's band
Yeah? Who was that?
Some guy on the radio station, something in Boston, public network. He said Snub Mosley is the fastest slide in the west.
You better believe it.
Did you get to make any of the soundings or anything like that?
I made one.
This is the patent for the slide? June 17, 1924. Here's another one, musical whistle. That isn't yours.
I had to have a search.
Yeah, yeah, I follow you.
What year did I have the search made?
It says: Unless you can point out inventive novelty in the above references, I am of the opinion that he has presented nothing patentable. He's a patent attorney, this guy.

The Mosley Slide Sax.
So, in other words, you never really
couldn't patent. So what, you're the only guy
using it, it really becomes the same way. Who's
going to go out and invent something like that?

We were going to put
it out, Rudy Muck.

Oh, but you didn't think
you could patent it?

Yeah, we could patent
it.

Why not? It's something
that's in use.

Yeah, we could patent
it.

What about the Sands?
You were working--you had the organo; where did
the organo come in? Is that the first time you
used the organo?

At the Frolic. That's
the first time I used the organo.
Had that just been
Yeah. It seems to me that's the first I heard of it.
This same guy, this Neal Tate, is the same guy that was working for you then?
At first I had another little guy and then Neal Tate came in.
Neal Tate was good.
He was really great. '55 is the Frolic, and I stayed at the Frolic for five years.
I know, I was there all the time. I was there a lot.
There sure used to be some fine things in there.

The guy at the Metropole, they tried to pull a fast one. We were pulling a lot of people away from the Metropole at one time and they offered me a job at the Metropole to come in there in the afternoon. I knew what they were going to do, I would have come out of there and they would have fired me after a month.
That's exactly what they would have done. I know that guy, that was Harriman, he was a real bastard.

That's what the idea was, because we were drawing too many people. I stayed in there from '55 to '60 and I was up at the--in '57 I went to the Windsor, up in the Catskills. I'd go up there for the summer and come back in the fall. I stayed at the Windsor for two years, '57 and '58 and '59 I went to Grossinger's. Then I came back to the Frolic. In fact, I did the Frolic until '60. Then in '60 I went to the Riviera, Rube Congris' Riviera, that was a wonderful, beautiful thing there. We really made a very rich man out of that fellow. In '62 I went into the Sands for two weeks and stayed the season, and the next season I asked for more money and I couldn't get it, so I went into the Atlantic Beach Hotel and
they gave me a contract for the next four years back at the Sands.
At the money you wanted?

At the money I wanted. They had so many other places, there was this place advertised the Roosevelt Motel, we played there in the winter. In '64 I did the World's Fair. I stayed there until time to go back to the Sands in April.
What place were you playing at the World's Fair?
A place called the Balcony in the Louisiana pavillon. It was Wonderful. Joe Jones was there on drums, Big Nick on sax.
Irstin Hawkins was there.
Was he?
Yeah.
(Inaudible) I had Keg Purnell with me, and Sy (inaudible). He stayed with me until he died. He was a wonderful drummer.
When did you first get him? What year?
I found him, when we went into Stuyvesant Casino and we were all gigging around, by myself.
No steady jobs?
That's the way I met Keg. When I went into the Frolic he stayed with me for eleven years.
I guess he's the best you ever had, next to A.G. Godley.
He was the best one I ever had, other than A.G. Godley; yeah.
He would have been great in the eight piece band. He was with Eddie Haywood all those years.
Yeah, he was with Eddie Haywood too.
You said Bob Carroll died; right?
Yeah.
Where was he from?
He's from Ohio.
How was this Hazel Diaz?
She wasn't working with you, was she?
No. They knew her.
They put her on the record with me.
You never really had a need for a girl singer working with you? You did all your own entertainment, you didn't need anything else.
That's right.
The only time you had somebody was when you had Evelyn White and the travelling show.
That's right.
That's '50.
And when I went overseas, touring Greenland and Newfoundland.
That's later on, in the sixties.
In the sixties; yeah. I went in the Sands in '62, the Atlantic Beach Hotel in '63, Sands, four, five and

six, but in between there--you see, the Sands was just a seasonal job, so in between there I would go to Greenland and on one of my trips I had Barbara Joy and another girl, this Jeri Dean--I must be lucky with singers, because she got to be the star of The Me That Nobody Knows and Me and Bessie, and also she was the queen of the automobile show about four years ago--four or five years ago--Jeri Dean, and of course Alberta Hunter; she did very well.
She certainly did.
She's doing better now than she's ever done; isn't she?
Oh yeah she is.
Some very interesting things happened.

I'm going to send you a list of all the records that Louie made from the time that we think he joined and to the time we think he left, we may find some others. A lot of that time when you were with him, he wasn't recording, he wasn't using his own band. Decca had him recording

with the Mills Brothers who was a small group and they had him recording with Andy Iona, they had him recording with Jimmy Dorsey's band; a lot of times he was not using his own band. You made all your records with him, clustered in a little bunch. I thought when you joined him I thought that he was still (inaudible), but I guess he wasn't.
No, no.
You were just doing theatres and one nighters.
I did a lot of one nighters, all the way across the country.
There's a tour that Leonard Fether went on the bus with at one point; I thought that was in '36, that should have been the time that you were in the band.
Maybe that's where I met Leonard; could be.
You played in New Orleans with Louie; that was the first time you ever played New Orleans.

I didn't (inaudible) We played every place--we played all over Louisiana, but I don't ever remember playing in New Orleans. We played Lake Charles, Louisiana and that's where I met the Whitman Sisters and that's where Willie Bryant was with the Whitman Sisters that time.
When you were playing in New Orleans, it was just a theatre date?
No, no, no, we didn't play a theatre date.
What was it, a dance?
We just played dance. We played at some racetrack, a great big place. And he packed them.

I got that picture of the band, but without Louie, all white suits, in Chicago, for the Mayor of Bronzeville. That's the first time I ever saw a picture of you with that band, so I knew you had to be in one.
I haven't got a picture of me with Louie.
Louie's not on it
though, it's everybody else in the band, but Louie; Biggy Madison, Charlie Holmes, Greeley, Louis Bacon, Ham Davis, Paul Barbara--
Am I on that?
You're on that; I have it. I have that; yeah. Mayor of Bronzeville it says.
Wasn't there a time when Louie--when Louie took off for Hollywood, didn't the band go back to work under Louis Russell's name for the time being?
No. They stayed right there in Kansas City. They waited in Kansas City until Louie came back.
Just doing nothing but laying around?
Louie didn't stay away but about two weeks.
Just two weeks?
That's all, maybe two weeks or so.
But in the meantime you
No, but that was fine with me because my folks were there.
In Kansas City?
All my father's people live there.
So you had no problem.

I had no problem at all; I was staying with my--they had a great big mansion there and I just had a ball. I was jamming a lot, I was playing my horn. Down on 18th Street, 18th and Bryant they had the Street's Hotel and we used to go down to the ballrooms and play too. We used to go everywhere.
Now with Fats, did Fats feature you much in his band?

I didn't get a chance to do too much with Fats. I did some--they featured me some, but that's one of the reasons I didn't stay. I was so accustomed to being free with Trent, I was completely free there--
(Side B of Tape 4 ends at this point.)

segments.chapter: Growing up in Little Rock
segments.title: Starting on trombone in the Gibbs High School band
segments.summary: A grandfather on the instrument committee lets him choose the trombone; he starts in the Little Rock high school band.

segments.chapter: Growing up in Little Rock
segments.title: Fellow trombonists in Little Rock and finding his own style
segments.summary: Happy Johnson and Will Parish are the only trombonists around; he practises day and night to avoid copying anyone, and the bandmaster raps him for adding notes.

segments.chapter: Growing up in Little Rock
segments.title: Little Rock's jazz scene and Sterling Todd's orchestra
segments.summary: The only jazz in town is Sterling Todd's Grove Street Orchestra, with no night clubs; talk of its members and wives.

segments.chapter: Trent's band: Arkansas, Dallas and the Adolphus
segments.title: Meeting Trent through Eugene Cook and a summer drug store job
segments.summary: Cook hears his swing solo at a parade and hires him; the band plays for tips outside a drug store in Arkansas until his mother sends the police.

segments.chapter: Trent's band: Arkansas, Dallas and the Adolphus
segments.title: Trent takes over the band and A.G. Godley joins
segments.summary: Trent becomes leader, brings in Joe Haymen and Swazey, replaces his cousin on drums with A.G., and they play a summer resort in Muskogee.

segments.chapter: Trent's band: Arkansas, Dallas and the Adolphus
segments.title: Trent's wealthy Fort Smith family and the band they bankrolled
segments.summary: Trent, from a family owning rows of rent houses, is more business-minded than Cook and keeps the band together near Little Rock.

segments.chapter: Trent's band: Arkansas, Dallas and the Adolphus
segments.title: Everyone had to read: stock arrangements and standards
segments.summary: Only stock arrangements, and everyone had to read and later also improvise in the co-op band.

segments.chapter: Trent's band: Arkansas, Dallas and the Adolphus
segments.title: Touring Eldorado, passing the hat and Andy Kirk's origins
segments.summary: On tour they pass the hat for food and rooms; talk of Louis Jordan's home town and Andy Kirk getting his band from the trumpeter.

segments.chapter: Trent's band: Arkansas, Dallas and the Adolphus
segments.title: Winning a tryout at the Dallas hotel: back elevator and Klan threat
segments.summary: A bellman and the manager's secretary get the band a two-week tryout at a whites-only hotel; they use the back elevator and the Klan plans trouble.

segments.chapter: Trent's band: Arkansas, Dallas and the Adolphus
segments.title: Local substitute bands and Don Bester across the street
segments.summary: Bands who filled in during the band's vacation fail; Troy Floyd and others spring up, and Don Bester opens at the Baker Hotel.

segments.chapter: Trent's band: Arkansas, Dallas and the Adolphus
segments.title: Band photograph: Haymen brothers, Holloway, Fielding and Trent's scrapbook
segments.summary: Identifies men in a photograph from the Plaza Hotel and talks about the missing scrapbook.

segments.chapter: Trent's band: Arkansas, Dallas and the Adolphus
segments.title: Holder let go as manager and his replacement
segments.summary: Holder is dismissed after losing the manager's job; the replacement is a decent player with a poor tone, and Chester Clark is praised.

segments.chapter: Trent's band: Arkansas, Dallas and the Adolphus
segments.title: Adding Chester Clark; where Holder came from and how he ended
segments.summary: Chester Clark joins during the hotel run; Holder came from Muskogee and later lost both legs and returned there.

segments.chapter: Trent's band: Arkansas, Dallas and the Adolphus
segments.title: Holder skims the band's raise and Mosley becomes manager
segments.summary: The hotel gives each man a $25 raise that Holder pockets until Trent asks; Mosley takes over as manager.

segments.chapter: Trent's band: Arkansas, Dallas and the Adolphus
segments.title: WFAA broadcasts, dance tours and a year and a half at the hotel
segments.summary: The band broadcasts on a powerful station, books its own dances at $75-90 a man, and stays a year and a half.

segments.chapter: Trent's band: Arkansas, Dallas and the Adolphus
segments.title: Respect from audiences and Bobby the drummer
segments.summary: The band has few race problems at the hotel and is treated like gods; the drummer Bobby drinks but is overlooked.

segments.chapter: Trent's band: Arkansas, Dallas and the Adolphus
segments.title: Co-op rehearsals and head arrangements
segments.summary: Each member leads rehearsals on a different day and sections are written collectively, making many into arrangers and leaders.
